cards.title: Does Resolution effectively polynomially simulate Extended Frege?
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic transformation R and fixed polynomials p,q such that, for every propositional formula F and every integer s≥1, R(F,1ˢ) outputs a CNF formula in at most p(|F|+s) bit operations, F is a tautology if and only if R(F,1ˢ) is unsatisfiable, and whenever F has an Extended Frege proof of length at most s, R(F,1ˢ) has a Resolution refutation of length at most q(|F|+s)?
cards.why: Determines whether allowing efficient preprocessing fundamentally changes the apparent gap between elementary clause reasoning and proof systems that can name arbitrary intermediate Boolean computations. This affects what proof-size separations say about algorithms for finding proofs.

progress.text: Pitassi and Santhanam define effective polynomial simulation and explicitly pose the Resolution-versus-Extended-Frege question.

cards.definitions: A propositional formula uses Boolean variables, negation ¬ and implication →, with the usual truth tables; other connectives are fixed abbreviations. A tautology is true under every Boolean assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. The empty clause is false. A Resolution refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each line being an input clause or the resolvent C∨D of earlier clauses C∨x and D∨¬x. Lines can be reused, so the proof is a directed acyclic derivation, not necessarily a tree. Fix Extended Frege as follows: ordinary Frege lines are substitution instances of A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), or follow by modus ponens from A and A→B. One may also introduce an extension axiom z↔B, where z is fresh, does not occur in the target F, and B uses only original variables and previously introduced extension variables. Here z↔B abbreviates (z→B)∧(B→z). The final line is F, containing no extension variables. Formulas, proofs and line references have explicit finite binary encodings; length counts the whole encoding. Standard alternative Frege bases and symbol-count conventions are polynomially equivalent. The input 1ˢ is a unary string, so the permitted time is polynomial in s, not log s. The transformation receives F and s but no EF proof. It must preserve the tautology/unsatisfiability equivalence for every F and every s, even if s is smaller than the shortest proof or F is not a tautology. Only the short-Resolution-refutation guarantee is conditional on an EF proof of length at most s. Resolution is represented by refuting a CNF, while Frege proves a tautology; this explicitly implements the source’s comparison of proof systems over their natural encodings.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of R,p,q satisfying all these conditions. The requested notion is effective polynomial simulation as in Definition 2.5 of the source. A polynomial procedure that converts a supplied EF proof is an additional, stronger guarantee and is not required. A lower bound on Resolution proofs of the original untransformed formula alone does not refute this claim.

context_blocks.title: Can preprocessing change the proof-size comparison?
context_blocks.text: Resolution is a basic way to certify that a set of clauses is inconsistent. Extended Frege additionally uses named intermediate formulas, allowing compact reuse of complicated expressions. The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

context_blocks.title: A Resolution step
context_blocks.text: From x∨y and ¬x, Resolution derives y. Together with the clause ¬y, it then derives the empty clause and certifies inconsistency. Larger derivations reuse earlier clauses. An extension variable, by contrast, can name a compound formula and be reused wherever that formula is needed.

context_blocks.title: Why the extra input matters
context_blocks.text: The transformation is given a proposed proof-size allowance s. It may spend polynomial time in that allowance, even if the statement itself is short. It must preserve correctness for all allowances, but it needs to guarantee a short output refutation only when an EF proof fits within the allowance. The actual proof is never supplied to it.

context_blocks.title: The known separation answers a different comparison
context_blocks.text: Ordinary polynomial simulation compares proofs of the same statement. Known Resolution lower bounds rule out ordinary simulation of Extended Frege. Effective simulation allows the statement to change through a correctness-preserving transformation, so those lower bounds do not automatically answer this question.

context_blocks.title: A later example of the distinction
context_blocks.text: Buss and Yolcu show that regular Resolution effectively simulates unrestricted Resolution, despite known exponential separations when both systems must use the same formula. Regular Resolution forbids resolving a variable twice along a derivation path. Their result demonstrates that the distinction has mathematical force, but does not provide an effective simulation of EF.

sentences: Resolution refutes inconsistent clauses, while Extended Frege permits named intermediate Boolean formulas.
Ordinary proof-size comparisons keep the statement fixed and separate these systems.
This question allows a polynomial-time transformation of the statement, given a unary bound on an EF proof’s length.
Whenever that bound is sufficient, the transformed CNF must have a comparably short Resolution refutation, while correctness must be preserved for every input.
An answer would clarify whether efficient preprocessing can overcome the proof-size gap between these systems.

cards.title: Bounded protocols for connected envy-free proportional cake cutting
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For every fixed integer n≥4, does there exist a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol Pₙ and a finite integer Bₙ such that, for every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations and all valid query answers, Pₙ uses at most Bₙ queries and returns disjoint connected bundles A₁,…,Aₙ satisfying μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for all i,j and μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for all i, while permitting unallocated cake?
cards.why: Asks whether discarded cake permits exact fairness together with geometric simplicity in finite interaction.

progress.text: Finite exact envy-free protocols are ruled out for complete connected allocation with n≥3.
Bounded partial-allocation protocols achieve exact proportionality for three connected recipients, and weaker connected guarantees for larger n.
General bounded protocols give connected partial allocations worth at least 1/(3n) per agent.
A preprint reports single-exponential queries for complete allocation with possibly fragmented bundles.

cards.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. In this question each Aᵢ must be one interval, up to ownership of its endpoints. The intervals may have gaps between them, and the residue [0,1]∖⋃ᵢAᵢ may be discarded. Envy is compared with other agents’ assigned intervals, not with the residue. Count every Eval and Cut call as one query. The bound Bₙ depends only on the fixed n and its protocol, never on the valuation profile or oracle responses. The statement permits a separate finite protocol for each n; it does not require Bₙ to be polynomial, and does not add an algorithm that generates all Pₙ.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a bounded protocol for every fixed n≥4, or prove that for at least one fixed n≥4 no deterministic protocol and finite bound satisfy the stated guarantees. Existence of a suitable division alone, a procedure that merely converges to one, approximate proportionality, or allowing an agent several intervals does not meet this target.

context_blocks.title: Fairness with one usable piece
context_blocks.text: A connected share is a single interval, as in a continuous appointment slot or one tract of land. Envy-freeness says each person prefers her own assigned interval to anyone else’s. Proportionality additionally protects the amount she receives: at least one n-th of her value for the whole resource.

context_blocks.title: Why disposal changes the question
context_blocks.text: With disposal, giving everyone nothing is envy-free. For example, agents with identical uniform values can each receive an interval of length 1/(2n), leaving half the cake unused; none envies another, but all receive less than their proportional share. The exact 1/n requirement excludes such wasteful outcomes.

context_blocks.title: The connected impossibility has a specific scope
context_blocks.text: Stromquist proves that no finite protocol can always allocate the entire cake envy-freely with one interval per agent once n≥3. This assumes complete allocation. Allowing residue is the change studied here, so that theorem does not refute this question.

context_blocks.title: Known partial-allocation guarantees
context_blocks.text: Waste Makes Haste gives a bounded connected envy-free proportional protocol for three agents in its density model. For four agents its connected guarantee is 1/7 instead of the required 1/4. Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded connected partial allocation with a 1/(3n) value guarantee in general. These results motivate the question but do not supply exact proportionality for all n≥4.

context_blocks.title: Later progress allows fragmented shares
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports a single-exponential query bound for complete envy-free allocation. Complete envy-freeness implies proportionality, but the output may contain multiple intervals per agent. It therefore does not answer this connected-piece question.

sentences: The cake is a divisible interval valued differently by each agent.
The desired division gives every agent one interval, eliminates envy, and guarantees at least one n-th of her value for the whole cake.
Unallocated cake is allowed, but it cannot reduce that proportionality guarantee.
Known connected partial protocols provide weaker guarantees for larger numbers of agents, while recent complete protocols allow fragmented shares.
The question is whether a fixed finite query bound can achieve all the requested properties for every fixed n≥4.

For each n, let Q(n) be the minimum integer B for which a deterministic finite protocol for n agents always returns such an allocation within B queries, for every valuation profile and all valid answers. Known bounded complete-allocation protocols imply that this set of B is nonempty; its least integer is attained. The requested complexity is the asymptotic order of Q(n), with exact fairness on every input and no average-case, error or expected-cost convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a function f(n), constants 0<c≤C and n₀ such that c f(n)≤Q(n)≤C f(n) for every n≥n₀. The upper bound must be realized by valid protocols and the lower bound must apply to every valid deterministic protocol in the stated model. Logarithmic or polynomial-factor gaps do not count as matching constant-factor bounds. This card uses the usual asymptotic interpretation of optimal query complexity, rather than asking for an exact integer query count at every n.

context_blocks.title: Two protections for each recipient
context_blocks.text: An agent should prefer her own bundle to every other assigned bundle, and should value it at least as much as one n-th of the original cake. These are separate conditions when some cake can remain unallocated. For identical uniform valuations, equal bundles of length 1/(2n) are envy-free but fail proportionality.

context_blocks.title: Why count questions?
context_blocks.text: A value measure can be arbitrarily complicated, so the protocol cannot read it as a finite table. Evaluation queries reveal interval values and cut queries reveal where a prescribed value ends. The cost measures how much exact interaction is necessary; it does not charge the local arithmetic or require the resulting bundles to be connected.

context_blocks.title: An established finite upper bound
context_blocks.text: Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded partial-allocation protocol meeting both envy-freeness and exact proportionality, with an exponential query bound. This already ensures Q(n) is finite. Their separate connected-piece result guarantees only a 1/(3n) share and addresses a different output requirement.

context_blocks.title: Recent complete-allocation progress also applies
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports n^{O(1)}2^n queries for a complete envy-free allocation. Such an allocation is also a permitted output here, since disposal is optional and completeness implies proportionality under nonnegative additive valuations. The reported bound is an upper bound for this problem, not a matching optimality result.

context_blocks.title: The value of allowing residue
context_blocks.text: Discarding some cake may make fairness easier to achieve, but the 1/n guarantee prevents an empty or arbitrarily small allocation. A tight query bound would show whether this freedom substantially reduces the information needed for exact fairness. A lower bound proved only for protocols that allocate everything would need a further argument to cover the more permissive target here.

Bounded complete-allocation protocols show that a finite uniform cut bound exists for every number of agents.
An exact cut bound is proved for an existential equal-length proportional variant, with different fairness and computational requirements.
A preprint reports single-exponential query complexity for complete envy-free allocation, without optimizing final cuts exactly.

cards.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. The output is a complete partition of the cake into bundles A₁,…,Aₙ. A final cut is an internal endpoint between two positive-length intervals assigned to different agents, after adjacent intervals with the same recipient have been merged. Thus an output with r such successive intervals uses r−1 final cuts; 0 and 1 do not count. Isolated endpoint ownership has no cost or fairness effect. Following the cited Stromquist paper, a point merely queried or marked during the protocol is not a final cut unless it is used as an allocation boundary. A protocol is finite if it terminates after finitely many queries on every profile and every valid sequence of answers. That query count may depend on the valuations and need not be bounded by a function of n; local computation must also terminate. In contrast, the number of final cuts must have the uniform bound c*(n). More formally, c*(n) is the minimum over nonnegative integers c for which such a finite protocol for n agents exists. Bounded complete-allocation protocols show this set is nonempty, so the integer minimum is attained. This question charges output cuts, not evaluation queries, queried marks, or total running time.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine c*(n) exactly for every n, proving both that a finite protocol attains the proposed uniform final-cut bound and that no finite protocol can guarantee a smaller one. A purely existential division with few cuts is insufficient unless a finite protocol can find it. Likewise, an upper bound on total queries does not prove optimality of final cuts.

context_blocks.title: Questions and physical fragmentation are different costs
context_blocks.text: A protocol can ask an agent to mark many candidate boundaries and then use only a few in the final division. This card follows the source’s explicit convention that cuts are the boundaries actually used. It asks how fragmented a division must become when it also has to be findable through finitely many queries.

context_blocks.title: A simple counting example
context_blocks.text: Suppose four successive intervals go to agents A, B, A and C. There are three final cuts, and A receives a disconnected bundle. If the first two intervals both went to A, their common boundary would disappear when those intervals were merged. Counting marks made during the search would be a different objective.

context_blocks.title: Existence does not imply a finite protocol
context_blocks.text: A complete connected envy-free division exists, using n−1 final cuts. Stromquist shows that no finite protocol can always find one for n≥3. Since every recipient in a complete envy-free division has positive value, an n−1-cut division would give exactly one interval per agent. Thus c*(n)≥n for n≥3, despite the existential n−1 bound.

context_blocks.title: The extremum is finite
context_blocks.text: For n=1 no cut is needed, and for n=2 the standard cut-and-choose protocol uses one final cut. General bounded protocols of Aziz and Mackenzie guarantee a finite number of cuts for every n. The September 2026 single-exponential query claim gives another reported upper bound, but its purpose is query complexity and it does not establish the least final-cut count.

context_blocks.title: A recent exact cut theorem has different requirements
context_blocks.text: The MFCS 2026 equal-length result determines an existential cut bound for proportional division with a prescribed physical length per agent. This question imposes exact envy-freeness and finite oracle computation, with no equal-length requirement. Those distinctions prevent transferring the numerical answer directly.

sentences: The whole cake must be allocated so that every agent prefers her own bundle to anyone else’s.
A finite query protocol may give an agent several intervals and may mark more candidate boundaries than it ultimately uses.
The objective is the smallest worst-case number of final allocation cuts for each n.
Connected envy-free divisions exist, but for n≥3 no finite protocol can always find one.
An exact answer would measure the unavoidable fragmentation of an envy-free division that can actually be found by finite interaction.

cards.context:
A protocol can ask an agent to mark many candidate boundaries and then use only a few in the final division. This card follows the source’s explicit convention that cuts are the boundaries actually used. It asks how fragmented a division must become when it also has to be findable through finitely many queries.

Suppose four successive intervals go to agents A, B, A and C. There are three final cuts, and A receives a disconnected bundle. If the first two intervals both went to A, their common boundary would disappear when those intervals were merged. Counting marks made during the search would be a different objective.

A complete connected envy-free division exists, using n−1 final cuts. Stromquist shows that no finite protocol can always find one for n≥3. Since every recipient in a complete envy-free division has positive value, an n−1-cut division would give exactly one interval per agent. Thus c*(n)≥n for n≥3, despite the existential n−1 bound.

For n=1 no cut is needed, and for n=2 the standard cut-and-choose protocol uses one final cut. General bounded protocols of Aziz and Mackenzie guarantee a finite number of cuts for every n. The September 2026 single-exponential query claim gives another reported upper bound, but its purpose is query complexity and it does not establish the least final-cut count.

The MFCS 2026 equal-length result determines an existential cut bound for proportional division with a prescribed physical length per agent. This question imposes exact envy-freeness and finite oracle computation, with no equal-length requirement. Those distinctions prevent transferring the numerical answer directly.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
